claim: Mutations in Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signaling pathway genes, for example, Suppressor of Fused (SUFU), drive granule neuron precursors (GNP) to form medulloblastomas (MBSHH).
source: Mutations in Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signaling pathway genes, for example, Suppressor of Fused (SUFU), drive granule neuron precursors (GNP) to form medulloblastomas (MBSHH).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the role of SHH pathway mutations in medulloblastoma formation.

claim: FGF5 signaling is integral for many infantile MBSHH cases.
source: In this study, we show that fibroblast growth factor 5 (FGF5) signaling is integral for many infantile MBSHH cases and that FGF5 expression is uniquely upregulated in infantile MBSHH tumors.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing FGF5 expression patterns in infantile MBSHH tumors and experimental evidence from mouse models.

claim: FGF5 expression is uniquely upregulated in infantile MBSHH tumors.
source: In this study, we show that fibroblast growth factor 5 (FGF5) signaling is integral for many infantile MBSHH cases and that FGF5 expression is uniquely upregulated in infantile MBSHH tumors.
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis from patient tumor samples shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mice lacking SUFU (Sufu-cKO) ectopically express Fgf5 specifically along the secondary fissure where GNPs harbor preneoplastic lesions.
source: Similarly, mice lacking SUFU (Sufu-cKO) ectopically express Fgf5 specifically along the secondary fissure where GNPs harbor preneoplastic lesions and show that FGFR signaling is also ectopically activated in this region.
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: FGFR signaling is ectopically activated in the secondary fissure region of Sufu-cKO mice.
source: Similarly, mice lacking SUFU (Sufu-cKO) ectopically express Fgf5 specifically along the secondary fissure where GNPs harbor preneoplastic lesions and show that FGFR signaling is also ectopically activated in this region.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining for phospho-Erk1/2 shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: Treatment with an FGFR antagonist rescues the severe GNP hyperplasia in Sufu-cKO mice.
source: Treatment with an FGFR antagonist rescues the severe GNP hyperplasia and restores cerebellar architecture.
evidence: Demonstrated by AZD4547 treatment experiments shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: Treatment with an FGFR antagonist restores cerebellar architecture in Sufu-cKO mice.
source: Treatment with an FGFR antagonist rescues the severe GNP hyperplasia and restores cerebellar architecture.
evidence: Shown by Nissl staining and immunofluorescence in Figure 3F-G.

claim: Direct inhibition of FGF signaling may be a promising and novel therapeutic candidate for infantile MBSHH.
source: Thus, direct inhibition of FGF signaling may be a promising and novel therapeutic candidate for infantile MBSHH.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the rescue experiments with FGFR antagonist.

claim: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant brain tumor in children.
source: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant brain tumor in children, with half of the cases diagnosed before the age of 5 (Ward et al., 2014; Ostrom et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ward et al., 2014 and Ostrom et al., 2016.

claim: Half of medulloblastoma cases are diagnosed before the age of 5.
source: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant brain tumor in children, with half of the cases diagnosed before the age of 5 (Ward et al., 2014; Ostrom et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ward et al., 2014 and Ostrom et al., 2016.

claim: Mutations in SUFU comprise approximately 30% of tumors in infants with Sonic Hedgehog-driven MB.
source: Mutations in Suppressor of Fused (SUFU) comprise approximately 30% of tumors in infants with Sonic Hedgehog-driven MB (MBSHH).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Infantile MBSHH has a worse prognosis than other MBSHH subtypes.
source: Infantile MBSHH, including those associated with SUFU mutations (MBSHH-SUFU), has a worse prognosis and higher rates of local recurrence than other MBSHH subtypes (Kool et al., 2014; Schwalbe et al., 2017; Guerrini-Rousseau et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kool et al., 2014; Schwalbe et al., 2017; Guerrini-Rousseau et al., 2018.

claim: Infantile MBSHH has higher rates of local recurrence than other MBSHH subtypes.
source: Infantile MBSHH, including those associated with SUFU mutations (MBSHH-SUFU), has a worse prognosis and higher rates of local recurrence than other MBSHH subtypes (Kool et al., 2014; Schwalbe et al., 2017; Guerrini-Rousseau et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kool et al., 2014; Schwalbe et al., 2017; Guerrini-Rousseau et al., 2018.

claim: Available SHH-targeted treatments for MBSHH act specifically on proteins upstream of SUFU.
source: Unfortunately, available SHH-targeted treatments for MBSHH act specifically on proteins upstream of SUFU and are therefore ineffective for MBSHH-SUFU patients (Kool et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kool et al., 2014.

claim: Available SHH-targeted treatments are ineffective for MBSHH-SUFU patients.
source: Unfortunately, available SHH-targeted treatments for MBSHH act specifically on proteins upstream of SUFU and are therefore ineffective for MBSHH-SUFU patients (Kool et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kool et al., 2014.

claim: SUFU acts as an intracellular modulator of SHH signaling.
source: SUFU acts as an intracellular modulator of SHH signaling (Matise and Wang, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matise and Wang, 2011.

claim: The Shh signaling pathway is initiated after the binding of extracellular Shh ligands to the transmembrane receptor Patched 1 (PTCH1).
source: Briefly, the Shh signaling pathway is initiated after the binding of extracellular Shh ligands to the transmembrane receptor Patched 1 (PTCH1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the SHH signaling pathway.

claim: Shh ligand binding to PTCH1 relieves PTCH1 inhibition of Smoothened (SMO).
source: This relieves PTCH1 inhibition of the transmembrane protein, Smoothened (SMO), and enables the initiation of a cascade of intracellular events promoting the activator function of the transcription factors, GLI1, GLI2, or GLI3.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the SHH signaling pathway.

claim: Sufu modulates Shh signaling by ensuring the stability of Gli transcription factors.
source: Sufu modulates Shh signaling by ensuring the stability of Gli transcription factors or by promoting the formation of the repressor forms of GLI2 (GLI2R) or GLI3 (GLI3R) (Chen et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2014.

claim: Sufu modulates Shh signaling by promoting the formation of the repressor forms of GLI2 (GLI2R) or GLI3 (GLI3R).
source: Sufu modulates Shh signaling by ensuring the stability of Gli transcription factors or by promoting the formation of the repressor forms of GLI2 (GLI2R) or GLI3 (GLI3R) (Chen et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2014.

claim: Loss of Sufu can lead to activation or repression of Shh signaling depending on the developmental context.
source: Thus, depending on the developmental context, loss of Sufu can lead to activation or repression of Shh signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the described mechanisms of SUFU function.

claim: SUFU dysfunction is associated with the abnormal development of granule neuron precursors (GNP).
source: In the developing cerebellum, SUFU dysfunction is associated with the abnormal development of granule neuron precursors (GNP), which account for MBSHH (Kim et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2018; Vanner et al., 2014; Kong et al., 2019; Vladoiu et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2019; Jiwani et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations: Kim et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2018; Vanner et al., 2014; Kong et al., 2019; Vladoiu et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2019; Jiwani et al., 2020.

claim: GNPs populate the external granule layer (EGL) along the cerebellar perimeter.
source: GNPs populate the external granule layer (EGL) along the cerebellar perimeter, where local SHH signals trigger GNP proliferation and differentiation at neonatal stages.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar development.

claim: Local SHH signals trigger GNP proliferation and differentiation at neonatal stages.
source: GNPs populate the external granule layer (EGL) along the cerebellar perimeter, where local SHH signals trigger GNP proliferation and differentiation at neonatal stages.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar development.

claim: Other mitogenic pathways can influence GNP behavior.
source: However, other mitogenic pathways can also influence GNP behavior (Leto et al., 2016), yet little is known about how SUFU interacts with these pathways.
evidence: Supported by citation to Leto et al., 2016.

claim: Little is known about how SUFU interacts with other mitogenic pathways.
source: However, other mitogenic pathways can also influence GNP behavior (Leto et al., 2016), yet little is known about how SUFU interacts with these pathways.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: FGF5 expression is upregulated in tumors of infantile MBSHH patients.
source: In this study, we examined the regulation of FGF signaling in MBSHH and identified upregulation of FGF5 expression in tumors of infantile MBSHH patients.
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ectopic expression of Fgf5 occurs in the neonatal cerebellum of mice lacking SUFU.
source: Similarly, we show ectopic expression of Fgf5 in the neonatal cerebellum of mice lacking SUFU, which correlates with the activation of FGF signaling in surrounding EGL-localized cells where GNPs accumulate.
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Ectopic Fgf5 expression correlates with the activation of FGF signaling in surrounding EGL-localized cells where GNPs accumulate.
source: Similarly, we show ectopic expression of Fgf5 in the neonatal cerebellum of mice lacking SUFU, which correlates with the activation of FGF signaling in surrounding EGL-localized cells where GNPs accumulate.
evidence: Demonstrated by phospho-Erk1/2 staining in Figure 3B-D.

claim: Acute pharmacological inhibition of FGF signaling results in near-complete rescue of GNP defects in Sufu-cKO mice.
source: Strikingly, acute pharmacological inhibition of FGF signaling results in near-complete rescue of these defects, including restoration of cerebellar histo-organization.
evidence: Demonstrated by AZD4547 treatment experiments in Figure 3E-G.

claim: FGF5 is a potential biomarker for a subset of patients with infantile MBSHH who may be responsive to FGFR-targeting therapies.
source: Thus, our findings identify FGF5 as a potential biomarker for a subset of patients with infantile MBSHH who may be responsive to FGFR-targeting therapies.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the data showing FGF5 upregulation in infantile MBSHH and rescue with FGFR inhibitor.

claim: Sufu LOF in neocortical progenitors results in FGF signaling activation to influence the specification and differentiation of neocortical excitatory neurons.
source: We previously reported that Sufu LOF in neocortical progenitors results in FGF signaling activation to influence the specification and differentiation of neocortical excitatory neurons (Yabut et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yabut et al., 2020.

claim: FGF5 expression is higher in MBSHH tumors compared to other MB subgroups.
source: Strikingly, our analyses show that FGF5 expression is higher in tumors, specifically from MBSHH patients, compared to other MB subgroups, with approximately 25% of MBSHH tumors exhibiting a twofold increase (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparative analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Approximately 25% of MBSHH tumors exhibit a twofold increase in FGF5 expression.
source: Strikingly, our analyses show that FGF5 expression is higher in tumors, specifically from MBSHH patients, compared to other MB subgroups, with approximately 25% of MBSHH tumors exhibiting a twofold increase (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparative analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: FGF5 is uniquely upregulated in MBSHH tumors from patients within the 0–3-year-old age group.
source: We also find that FGF5 is uniquely upregulated in MBSHH tumors from patients within the 0–3-year-old age group, but not patients within the same age group in other MB subtypes (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by age-stratified gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Infantile tumors, largely belonging to the SHHβ and SHHγ subgroups, exhibit higher FGF5 levels compared to tumors from children (SHHα) or adults (SHHδ).
source: Infantile tumors, largely belonging to the SHHβ and SHHγ subgroups (Cavalli et al., 2017), exhibit higher FGF5 levels compared to tumors from children (SHHα) or adults (SHHδ) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by subgroup-stratified gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The proportion of SHHβ and SHHγ tumors with relatively high levels of FGF5 is significantly increased (~30%) compared to other MBSHH subgroups.
source: By all measures, the proportion of SHHβ and SHHγ tumors with relatively high levels of FGF5 is significantly increased (~30%) compared to other MBSHH subgroups (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: FGF signaling is specifically disrupted in infantile-onset MBSHH.
source: Taken together, these findings strongly suggest that FGF signaling is specifically disrupted in infantile-onset MBSHH.
evidence: This is inferred from the FGF5 expression patterns observed in infantile MBSHH tumors.

claim: FGF signaling has been implicated in cerebellar development, particularly in granule neuron development.
source: FGF signaling has been implicated in cerebellar development, particularly in granule neuron development (Yaguchi et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2011), leading us to wonder if and how aberrant FGF signaling may be contributing to the oncogenicity of GNPs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Yaguchi et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2011.

claim: Sufu-cKO mice exhibit profound defects in cerebellar development.
source: Sufu-cKO mice exhibit profound defects in cerebellar development.
evidence: Demonstrated by morphological and immunohistochemical analyses shown in Figure 2.

claim: At P0, there is a visible increase in measured cerebellar size in Sufu-cKO cerebellum compared to controls.
source: At P0, a time point at which GNP proliferation and differentiation is ongoing, there is a visible increase in measured cerebellar size and expansion of Pax6-positive (Pax6+) GNPs in the EGL of Sufu-cKO cerebellum compared to controls (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At P0, there is expansion of Pax6-positive (Pax6+) GNPs in the EGL of Sufu-cKO cerebellum compared to controls.
source: At P0, a time point at which GNP proliferation and differentiation is ongoing, there is a visible increase in measured cerebellar size and expansion of Pax6-positive (Pax6+) GNPs in the EGL of Sufu-cKO cerebellum compared to controls (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence and quantification shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The expansion of Pax6+ GNPs specifically localizes along the secondary fissure (EGL region B) in the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum.
source: Notably, the expansion of Pax6+ GNPs specifically localizes along the secondary fissure (EGL region B, arrow in Figure 2A) compared to other EGL areas (EGL regions A and C) in the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by regional quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Fgf5 is highly expressed immediately adjacent to the presumptive secondary fissure in the P0 control cerebellum.
source: In situ hybridization (ISH) using Fgf5-specific riboprobes show high expression of Fgf5 (Fgf5high) immediately adjacent to the presumptive secondary fissure in the P0 control cerebellum (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There is an expansion of Fgf5high expression regions in the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum.
source: Strikingly, in the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum, there is an expansion of Fgf5high expression regions (Figure 2E), coinciding with areas near the secondary fissure where GNP expansion is most severe (Figure 2A and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The expansion of Fgf5high expression regions coincides with areas near the secondary fissure where GNP expansion is most severe.
source: Strikingly, in the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum, there is an expansion of Fgf5high expression regions (Figure 2E), coinciding with areas near the secondary fissure where GNP expansion is most severe (Figure 2A and D).
evidence: This is a correlation observed between Fgf5 expression and GNP expansion patterns.

claim: Fgf5-expressing cells are largely excluded from the EGL of the control cerebellum.
source: Further, while Fgf5-expressing (FGF5+) cells are largely excluded from the EGL of the control cerebellum, a substantial number of Fgf5+ cells are ectopically localized in the EGL region B of the Sufu-cKO cerebellum (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: A substantial number of Fgf5+ cells are ectopically localized in the EGL region B of the Sufu-cKO cerebellum.
source: Further, while Fgf5-expressing (FGF5+) cells are largely excluded from the EGL of the control cerebellum, a substantial number of Fgf5+ cells are ectopically localized in the EGL region B of the Sufu-cKO cerebellum (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Fgf5 mRNA molecules are visibly higher in Fgf5-expressing cells in the Sufu-cKO EGL.
source: Fgf5 mRNA molecules are visibly higher in Fgf5-expressing cells in the Sufu-cKO EGL, while Fgf5 expression is largely absent in the deeper EGL regions (outlined cells within boxed regions in Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Fgf5 expression is largely absent in the deeper EGL regions of the Sufu-cKO cerebellum.
source: Fgf5 mRNA molecules are visibly higher in Fgf5-expressing cells in the Sufu-cKO EGL, while Fgf5 expression is largely absent in the deeper EGL regions (outlined cells within boxed regions in Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2F.

claim: FGF5 is a ligand for fibroblast growth factor receptors 1 (FGFR1) and 2 (FGFR2).
source: FGF5 is a ligand for fibroblast growth factor receptors 1 (FGFR1) and 2 (FGFR2), both of which are expressed in the developing cerebellum, particularly in IGL regions where Fgf5-expressing cells localize (Clements et al., 1993; Ornitz et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clements et al., 1993; Ornitz et al., 1996.

claim: FGFR1 and FGFR2 are expressed in the developing cerebellum, particularly in IGL regions where Fgf5-expressing cells localize.
source: FGF5 is a ligand for fibroblast growth factor receptors 1 (FGFR1) and 2 (FGFR2), both of which are expressed in the developing cerebellum, particularly in IGL regions where Fgf5-expressing cells localize (Clements et al., 1993; Ornitz et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clements et al., 1993; Ornitz et al., 1996.

claim: The binding of FGF5 to FGFR1 and FGFR2 triggers the activation of multiple intracellular signaling pathways, including the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway.
source: The binding of FGF5 to these receptors triggers the activation of multiple intracellular signaling pathways, including the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, to control cellular activities driving NSC progression (Figure 3A; Ornitz and Itoh, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ornitz and Itoh, 2015 and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: There is increased MAPK activity in the EGL of the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum.
source: Immunostaining with antibodies to detect MAPK pathway activation reveals increased MAPK activity in the EGL of the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum.
evidence: Demonstrated by phospho-Erk1/2 immunostaining shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The abnormally expanded EGL of the secondary fissure in the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum shows an increase in pErk1/2+ cells.
source: Regional distribution of cells labeled with phospho-Erk1/2 (pErk1/2+), a marker for activated MAPK signaling, shows that the abnormally expanded EGL of the secondary fissure in the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum increase in these cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There is a significant increase in pERK1/2+ cells in proliferative regions of the Sufu-cKO cerebellum compared to controls.
source: We quantified the number of pERK1/2+ cells in proliferative regions defined by dense Ki-67-labeled cells and found a significant increase in pERK1/2+ cells compared to controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Many pERK1/2+ cells are also proliferative as indicated by Ki-67 labeling.
source: Many pERK1/2+ cells are also proliferative as indicated by Ki-67 labeling (boxed areas, Figure 3B) and the numbers of these dual labeled cells were significantly higher in the Sufu-cKO cerebellum compared to controls (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by double-labeling immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3B and quantification in Figure 3D.

claim: The numbers of pERK1/2+ and Ki-67+ dual labeled cells are significantly higher in the Sufu-cKO cerebellum compared to controls.
source: Many pERK1/2+ cells are also proliferative as indicated by Ki-67 labeling (boxed areas, Figure 3B) and the numbers of these dual labeled cells were significantly higher in the Sufu-cKO cerebellum compared to controls (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The increase in Fgf5 expression correlates with the activation of FGF signaling in GNPs.
source: These findings indicate that the increase in Fgf5 expression correlates with the activation of FGF signaling in GNPs and demonstrates a likely role in regulating the abnormal proliferation and pre-neoplastic lesion in mutant mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between Fgf5 expression and pErk1/2 activation.

claim: FGF signaling likely plays a role in regulating the abnormal proliferation and pre-neoplastic lesion in Sufu-cKO mice.
source: These findings indicate that the increase in Fgf5 expression correlates with the activation of FGF signaling in GNPs and demonstrates a likely role in regulating the abnormal proliferation and pre-neoplastic lesion in mutant mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between Fgf5 expression, FGF signaling activation, and GNP hyperplasia.

claim: GLI protein levels in the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum show a marked reduction of GLI1, GLI2, GLI3, and PTCH1 levels.
source: Surprisingly, GLI protein levels in the P0 control and Sufu-cKO cerebellum show a marked reduction of GLI1, GLI2, GLI3, and PTCH1 levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1); this is inconsistent with elevated SHH signaling we anticipated in the absence of SUFU.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reduction in GLI protein levels is inconsistent with elevated SHH signaling anticipated in the absence of SUFU.
source: Surprisingly, GLI protein levels in the P0 control and Sufu-cKO cerebellum show a marked reduction of GLI1, GLI2, GLI3, and PTCH1 levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1); this is inconsistent with elevated SHH signaling we anticipated in the absence of SUFU.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Western blot data in relation to expected SHH signaling activity.

claim: Shh signaling activity is absent or very low throughout the entire P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum.
source: In these mice, Shh signaling activity is absent or very low throughout the entire P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum but is highly active in a region-specific manner in controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by Gli1-LacZ reporter activity shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Shh signaling is highly active in a region-specific manner in P0 control cerebellum.
source: In these mice, Shh signaling activity is absent or very low throughout the entire P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum but is highly active in a region-specific manner in controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by Gli1-LacZ reporter activity shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: LacZ+ cells are completely absent in EGL region B and adjacent areas of the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum.
source: Furthermore, while some LacZ+ cells are detectable in EGL regions A and C and adjacent ML and IGL, LacZ+ cells are completely absent in EGL region B and adjacent areas of the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Gli1-LacZ reporter activity shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The accumulation of GNPs does not rely on active Shh signaling, particularly in Region B.
source: These findings indicate that the accumulation of GNPs does not rely on active Shh signaling, particularly in Region B, where there is a severe expansion of GNPs in the absence of SUFU.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of Gli1-LacZ reporter activity in Region B despite GNP expansion.

claim: AZD4547 treatment results in near complete rescue of the GNP phenotype by P7 in the Sufu-cKO cerebellum.
source: Strikingly, AZD4547 treatment results in near complete rescue of the GNP phenotype by P7 in the Sufu-cKO cerebellum, displaying a cerebellar morphology indistinguishable from controls with normal foliation and cellular organization (Figure 3F).
evidence: Demonstrated by Nissl staining shown in Figure 3F.

claim: AZD4547-treated P7 Sufu-cKO cerebellum displays a cerebellar morphology indistinguishable from controls with normal foliation and cellular organization.
source: Strikingly, AZD4547 treatment results in near complete rescue of the GNP phenotype by P7 in the Sufu-cKO cerebellum, displaying a cerebellar morphology indistinguishable from controls with normal foliation and cellular organization (Figure 3F).
evidence: Demonstrated by Nissl staining shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In AZD4547-treated P7 Sufu-cKO mice, proliferating Ki-67+ cells largely exclusively localize in the EGL.
source: Indeed, in the cerebellum of AZD4547 -treated P7 Sufu-cKO mice, proliferating Ki-67+ cells largely exclusively localize in the EGL while NeuN+ cells densely pack the IGL and not the EGL (Figure 3G).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3G.

claim: In AZD4547-treated P7 Sufu-cKO mice, NeuN+ cells densely pack the IGL and not the EGL.
source: Indeed, in the cerebellum of AZD4547 -treated P7 Sufu-cKO mice, proliferating Ki-67+ cells largely exclusively localize in the EGL while NeuN+ cells densely pack the IGL and not the EGL (Figure 3G).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3G.

claim: NeuN expression appears in cells localized at the border of the EGL and ML in AZD4547-treated Sufu-cKO mice, where Ki-67+ cells are absent.
source: Notably, NeuN expression appears in cells localized at the border of the EGL and ML, where Ki-67+ cells are absent, indicating that post-mitotic cells successfully began differentiation as observed in controls (boxed regions, Figure 3G).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Post-mitotic cells successfully began differentiation in AZD4547-treated Sufu-cKO mice as observed in controls.
source: Notably, NeuN expression appears in cells localized at the border of the EGL and ML, where Ki-67+ cells are absent, indicating that post-mitotic cells successfully began differentiation as observed in controls (boxed regions, Figure 3G).
evidence: This is inferred from the NeuN expression pattern in AZD4547-treated mice.

claim: Inhibition of FGF signaling in proliferating GNPs of the Sufu-cKO cerebellum ensures normal progression of GNP differentiation.
source: Thus, our findings confirm that inhibition of FGF signaling in proliferating GNPs of the Sufu-cKO cerebellum ensure normal progression of GNP differentiation.
evidence: This is concluded from the rescue experiments with AZD4547.

claim: FGF signaling plays a critical role in driving GNP hyperplasia.
source: Our findings indicate a critical role for FGF signaling in driving GNP hyperplasia, making GNPs vulnerable to neoplastic lesions, resulting in tumorigenesis when SUFU is absent in the developing cerebellum.
evidence: This is concluded from the correlation between FGF signaling activation and GNP hyperplasia, and the rescue with FGFR inhibitor.

claim: FGF signaling makes GNPs vulnerable to neoplastic lesions when SUFU is absent in the developing cerebellum.
source: Our findings indicate a critical role for FGF signaling in driving GNP hyperplasia, making GNPs vulnerable to neoplastic lesions, resulting in tumorigenesis when SUFU is absent in the developing cerebellum.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of DNA damage markers and the tumor formation in Sufu;Trp53-dKO mice.

claim: Pax6+ GNPs within the neonatal Sufu-cKO EGL display an increase in double-strand breaks, especially in region B.
source: Indeed, we find that Pax6+ GNPs within the neonatal Sufu-cKO EGL display an increase in double-strand breaks, especially in region B (DSBs; Figure 4A and B), as detected by immunostaining for phosphorylated H2AX (γH2AX), an early marker for DSBs (Mah et al., 2010).
evidence: Demonstrated by γH2AX immunostaining shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Tumors do not readily form in the Sufu-cKO cerebellum.
source: Nevertheless, as previously reported, tumors do not readily form in the Sufu-cKO cerebellum (Yin et al., 2019), indicating either timely repair of DSBs or the induction of apoptosis in GNPs with significant genomic instability.
evidence: Supported by citation to Yin et al., 2019.

claim: The absence of tumor formation in Sufu-cKO cerebellum indicates either timely repair of DSBs or the induction of apoptosis in GNPs with significant genomic instability.
source: Nevertheless, as previously reported, tumors do not readily form in the Sufu-cKO cerebellum (Yin et al., 2019), indicating either timely repair of DSBs or the induction of apoptosis in GNPs with significant genomic instability.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of DNA damage without tumor formation.

claim: There is a significantly higher number of cells double-labeled with cleaved Caspase 3 (CC3) and γH2AX in EGL regions A and B of Sufu-cKO cerebellum.
source: Indeed, double-labeling with cleaved Caspase 3 (CC3) and γH2AX shows a significantly higher number of double-labeled cells in EGL regions A and B (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by double-labeling immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Trp53 is a downstream target of DSB repair pathways that mediates cell death to suppress tumor formation.
source: Among the downstream targets of DSB repair pathways is Trp53, which, when activated, mediates cell death to suppress tumor formation (Gao et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gao et al., 2000.

claim: Trp53 protein is present but significantly reduced in the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum.
source: In the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum, Trp53 protein is present, albeit significantly reduced (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The reduction in Trp53 may be driving an increase in DSBs, yet it is still sufficient to induce apoptotic pathways.
source: The reduction in Trp53 may be driving an increase in DSBs, yet it is still sufficient to induce apoptotic pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of both DNA damage and apoptotic markers.

claim: Conditional ablation of both Trp53 and Sufu in GNPs results in the formation of massive tumors in the cerebellum within 2 months after birth.
source: Supporting this, conditional ablation of both Trp53 and Sufu in GNPs (hGFAP-Cre;Sufufl/fl;Trp53fl/fl or Sufu;Trp53-dKO) results in the formation of massive tumors in the cerebellum within 2 months after birth (Figure 4F), indicating the failure to activate critical apoptotic pathways.
evidence: Demonstrated by H&E staining shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Tumor formation in Sufu;Trp53-dKO mice indicates the failure to activate critical apoptotic pathways.
source: Supporting this, conditional ablation of both Trp53 and Sufu in GNPs (hGFAP-Cre;Sufufl/fl;Trp53fl/fl or Sufu;Trp53-dKO) results in the formation of massive tumors in the cerebellum within 2 months after birth (Figure 4F), indicating the failure to activate critical apoptotic pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the tumor formation when both Sufu and Trp53 are deleted.

claim: Tumors do not form in mice lacking Trp53 alone.
source: However, tumors do not form in mice lacking Trp53 (Marino et al., 2000) or Sufu alone (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marino et al., 2000 and H&E staining shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Tumors do not form in mice lacking Sufu alone.
source: However, tumors do not form in mice lacking Trp53 (Marino et al., 2000) or Sufu alone (Figure 4F).
evidence: Demonstrated by H&E staining shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In the absence of SUFU, the failure of GNPs to transition into fully differentiated granule neurons compromises genomic stability.
source: These findings suggest that in the absence of SUFU, the failure of GNPs to transition into fully differentiated granule neurons compromises genomic stability and renders GNPs extremely vulnerable to tumor formation with a second molecular hit.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of DNA damage in Sufu-cKO and tumor formation in Sufu;Trp53-dKO mice.

claim: In the absence of SUFU, GNPs are extremely vulnerable to tumor formation with a second molecular hit.
source: These findings suggest that in the absence of SUFU, the failure of GNPs to transition into fully differentiated granule neurons compromises genomic stability and renders GNPs extremely vulnerable to tumor formation with a second molecular hit.
evidence: This is inferred from the tumor formation in Sufu;Trp53-dKO mice but not in single mutants.

claim: The neonatal cerebellum of Sufu-cKO displays EGL expansion due to excess proliferative (Ki-67+) and Pax6+ cells in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum.
source: As expected, the neonatal cerebellum of Sufu-cKO displays EGL expansion due to excess proliferative (Ki-67+) and Pax6+ cells in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum but not in Trp53-cKO and control cerebelli (Figure 4G).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4G.

claim: EGL expansion does not occur in Trp53-cKO and control cerebelli.
source: As expected, the neonatal cerebellum of Sufu-cKO displays EGL expansion due to excess proliferative (Ki-67+) and Pax6+ cells in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum but not in Trp53-cKO and control cerebelli (Figure 4G).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Expansion of Pax6+ GNPs in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO is most severe along the secondary fissure (EGL region B).
source: Further expansion of Pax6+ GNPs in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO is also most severe along the secondary fissure (EGL region B) compared to other EGL areas (EGL regions A and C) of the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dkO cerebellum (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: ISH for Fgf5 in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum shows ectopic Fgf5 expression.
source: As with our observations in the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum, ISH for Fgf5 in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum shows ectopic Fgf5 expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Fgf5+ cells are expanded anteriorly and detected specifically around the secondary fissure of the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum.
source: Particularly, Fgf5+ cells are expanded anteriorly and detected specifically around the secondary fissure of the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum (Figure 4I).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4I.

claim: There is ectopic MAPK signaling activity in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum.
source: There is also ectopic MAPK signaling activity in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum, with significantly higher numbers of pErk1/2+ cells within the EGL, many of which are proliferative as marked by co-labeling with Ki-67, within the expanded EGL of the secondary fissure (Figure 4J).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4J.

claim: There are significantly higher numbers of pErk1/2+ cells within the EGL of the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum.
source: There is also ectopic MAPK signaling activity in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum, with significantly higher numbers of pErk1/2+ cells within the EGL, many of which are proliferative as marked by co-labeling with Ki-67, within the expanded EGL of the secondary fissure (Figure 4J).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Many pErk1/2+ cells in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum are proliferative as marked by co-labeling with Ki-67.
source: There is also ectopic MAPK signaling activity in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum, with significantly higher numbers of pErk1/2+ cells within the EGL, many of which are proliferative as marked by co-labeling with Ki-67, within the expanded EGL of the secondary fissure (Figure 4J).
evidence: Demonstrated by double-labeling immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Ectopic Fgf5 expression triggers FGF signaling in GNPs in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum.
source: These findings indicate that, as in the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum, ectopic Fgf5 expression triggers FGF signaling in GNPs in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum and may facilitate oncogenic transformation and tumor growth of GNPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between Fgf5 expression and FGF signaling activation in Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum.

claim: Ectopic Fgf5 expression may facilitate oncogenic transformation and tumor growth of GNPs in Sufu;Trp53-dKO mice.
source: These findings indicate that, as in the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum, ectopic Fgf5 expression triggers FGF signaling in GNPs in the P0 Sufu;Trp53-dKO cerebellum and may facilitate oncogenic transformation and tumor growth of GNPs.
evidence: This is speculative based on the correlation between Fgf5 expression and tumor formation.

claim: The combinatorial effects of oncogenic SUFU mutations and other concurrent developmental signaling pathways make GNPs vulnerable to oncogenic transformation leading to infantile MBSHH.
source: Our studies identify a mechanism by which the combinatorial effects of oncogenic SUFU mutations and other concurrent developmental signaling pathways make GNPs vulnerable to oncogenic transformation leading to infantile MBSHH.
evidence: This is the main conclusion synthesized from all the experimental findings.

claim: Ectopic Fgf5 expression correlates with an increase in FGF signaling in areas where proliferating GNPs reside.
source: Using mice lacking Sufu in GNPs, we find that ectopic Fgf5 expression correlates with an increase in FGF signaling, particularly in areas where proliferating GNPs reside, resulting in GNP hyperplasia, preneoplastic lesions, and patterning defects.
evidence: Demonstrated by the spatial correlation between Fgf5 expression and pErk1/2 activation shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Ectopic Fgf5 expression results in GNP hyperplasia, preneoplastic lesions, and patterning defects.
source: Using mice lacking Sufu in GNPs, we find that ectopic Fgf5 expression correlates with an increase in FGF signaling, particularly in areas where proliferating GNPs reside, resulting in GNP hyperplasia, preneoplastic lesions, and patterning defects.
evidence: Demonstrated by morphological and molecular analyses shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: Inhibition of Fgf signaling through pharmacological blockade of FGFR1-3 prevents hyperplasia and associated cerebellar architectural abnormalities.
source: Inhibition of Fgf signaling through pharmacological blockade of FGFR1-3 prevents hyperplasia and associated cerebellar architectural abnormalities.
evidence: Demonstrated by AZD4547 treatment experiments shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: FGF-targeting compounds may be a promising therapeutic option for infantile MBSHH patients.
source: These findings indicate that FGF-targeting compounds may be a promising therapeutic option for infantile MBSHH patients, with elevated levels of FGF5 in tumor tissues acting as a potential biomarker.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the rescue experiments and FGF5 expression in patient tumors.

claim: Elevated levels of FGF5 in tumor tissues may act as a potential biomarker for infantile MBSHH.
source: These findings indicate that FGF-targeting compounds may be a promising therapeutic option for infantile MBSHH patients, with elevated levels of FGF5 in tumor tissues acting as a potential biomarker.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the FGF5 expression patterns in patient tumors.

claim: Expansion of Pax6+ GNPs in the newborn Sufu-cKO cerebellum occurs in the posterior/ventral regions of the cerebellar hemispheres where infantile MB tumors typically arise.
source: Expansion of Pax6+ GNPs in the newborn Sufu-cKO cerebellum (Figure 2) occurs in the posterior/ventral regions of the cerebellar hemispheres where infantile MB tumors typically arise (Tan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tan et al., 2018 and data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Posterior/ventral subregions of the cerebellar hemispheres have low levels of GLI1 reporter activity, PTCH1 expression, and SHH ligand expression.
source: Interestingly, these subregions have low levels of GLI1 reporter activity, PTCH1 expression, and SHH ligand expression (Corrales et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Corrales et al., 2004.

claim: Spatially distinct regulation of granule neuron development by SUFU may rely on non-canonical SHH signaling beyond SMO or through yet undefined downstream interactions.
source: Spatially distinct regulation of granule neuron development by SUFU may, therefore, rely on non-canonical SHH signaling beyond SMO or through yet undefined downstream interactions, resulting in control of FGF signaling activity.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed patterns of SHH and FGF signaling.

claim: Ectopic expression of FGF ligands, Fgf8 and Fgf15, are associated with degradation of GLI3R because of Sufu deletion.
source: Similarly, in previous studies, ectopic expression of FGF ligands, Fgf8 and Fgf15, are associated with degradation of GLI3R because of Sufu deletion, resulting in regional patterning and precursor specification and differentiation defects (Kim et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2018; Jiwani et al., 2020; Yabut et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2018; Jiwani et al., 2020; Yabut et al., 2020.

claim: SUFU acts at the intersection of SHH and FGF signaling to modulate GNP behavior.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that SUFU acts at the intersection of SHH and FGF signaling to modulate GNP behavior (as summarized in our working model in Figure 5).
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: SUFU exerts its role via stabilization of GLI transcription factors.
source: We postulate that SUFU exerts this role via stabilization of GLI transcription factors since we observed a decrease in GLI1, GLI2, and GLI3 protein level in the newborn Sufu-cKO cerebellum.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed decrease in GLI protein levels.

claim: Reducing GLI2 levels rescued GNP hyperplasia and patterning defects in the Sufu-cKO neonatal cerebellum.
source: Supporting this, Yin et al., 2019 found that reducing GLI2 levels rescued GNP hyperplasia and patterning defects in the Sufu-cKO neonatal cerebellum.
evidence: Supported by citation to Yin et al., 2019.

claim: In the wildtype cerebellum, Fgf5-expressing cells localize within the IGL surrounding the secondary fissure at P0.
source: In the wildtype cerebellum, Fgf5-expressing cells localize within the IGL surrounding the secondary fissure at P0 (Figure 4B; Ozawa et al., 1996; Hattori et al., 1997; Yaguchi et al., 2009) where GLI1 reporter activity (Figure 4A), and SHH and PTCH1 expression are lowest (Corrales et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ozawa et al., 1996; Hattori et al., 1997; Yaguchi et al., 2009; Corrales et al., 2004 and data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: By P4, Fgf5 expression is detected in cells within the IGL throughout the cerebellum.
source: By P4, Fgf5 expression is detected in cells within the IGL throughout the cerebellum (Yaguchi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yaguchi et al., 2009.

claim: By P14, Fgf5 is no longer detected in the IGL or other cerebellar regions.
source: However, by P14, a time point at which most granule neurons have differentiated, Fgf5 is no longer detected in the IGL or other cerebellar regions per Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas (Allen Institute for Brain Science, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Allen Institute for Brain Science, 2004.

claim: The strict spatiotemporal expression of Fgf5 strongly supports a stage-specific role for regulating GNP development, particularly along the secondary fissure.
source: The strict spatiotemporal expression of Fgf5 strongly supports a stage-specific role for regulating GNP development, particularly along the secondary fissure, to ensure timely differentiation and maturation of granule neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal and spatial expression patterns of Fgf5.

claim: Deregulation of Fgf5 expression correlates with the continued uncontrolled proliferation of GNPs that have failed to differentiate normally.
source: Indeed, as we observed in the P0 Sufu-cKO cerebellum, deregulation of Fgf5 expression correlates with the continued uncontrolled proliferation of GNPs that have failed to differentiate normally.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between ectopic Fgf5 expression and GNP hyperplasia.

claim: The findings are contrary to previous reports of the proliferation-suppressive roles of FGFs, particularly FGF2, in GNPs specifically carrying Ptch1 mutations.
source: Our findings are contrary to previous reports of the proliferation-suppressive roles of FGFs, particularly FGF2, in GNPs specifically carrying Ptch1 mutations (Fogarty et al., 2007; Emmenegger et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fogarty et al., 2007; Emmenegger et al., 2013.

claim: The newborn Sufu-cKO cerebellum still expresses PTCH1 and exhibits reduced GLI1, GLI2, and GLI3 protein levels.
source: However, in contrast to the Ptch1-cKO cerebellum, the newborn Sufu-cKO cerebellum still expresses PTCH1 and exhibits reduced GLI1, GLI2, and GLI3 protein levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Key molecular differences between Sufu-cKO and Ptch1-cKO may activate unique signaling networks in Sufu-cKO GNPs.
source: These key molecular differences may activate unique signaling networks in Sufu-cKO GNPs.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the molecular differences observed.

claim: 18 FGF ligands differ significantly in molecular features and binding specificities to distinct combinations of FGFR splice variants.
source: Additionally, 18 FGF ligands differ significantly in molecular features and binding specificities to distinct combinations of FGFR splice variants (Ornitz and Itoh, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ornitz and Itoh, 2015.

claim: Unlike FGF2, which acts in an autocrine manner, FGF5 can exert both autocrine and paracrine functions.
source: For example, unlike FGF2, which acts in an autocrine manner, FGF5 can exert both autocrine and paracrine functions, bind different combinations of FGFRs, and is dynamically expressed in distinct regions of the developing cerebellum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FGF ligand functions.

claim: FGF5 can bind different combinations of FGFRs.
source: For example, unlike FGF2, which acts in an autocrine manner, FGF5 can exert both autocrine and paracrine functions, bind different combinations of FGFRs, and is dynamically expressed in distinct regions of the developing cerebellum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FGF5 receptor binding.

claim: FGF5 is dynamically expressed in distinct regions of the developing cerebellum.
source: For example, unlike FGF2, which acts in an autocrine manner, FGF5 can exert both autocrine and paracrine functions, bind different combinations of FGFRs, and is dynamically expressed in distinct regions of the developing cerebellum.
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Fgf5 overexpression is known to drive cancer development and progression, including brain tumors.
source: Thus, in-depth studies are needed to elucidate the exact mechanisms triggered by abnormally high levels of FGF5 in the developing cerebellum, particularly since Fgf5 overexpression is known to drive cancer development and progression, including brain tumors (Allerstorfer et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Allerstorfer et al., 2008.

claim: The high occurrence of SUFU mutations in infantile MB indicates the selective vulnerability of the developing cerebellum to the neoplastic effects of SUFU dysfunction.
source: The high occurrence of SUFU mutations in infantile MB indicates the selective vulnerability of the developing cerebellum to the neoplastic effects of SUFU dysfunction.
evidence: This is inferred from the epidemiological pattern of SUFU mutations in infantile MB.

claim: The timing of SUFU LOF is critical for cerebellar defects.
source: Notably, the timing of SUFU LOF is critical; conditional deletion of Sufu in neural stem cells before granule neuron specification (using the hGFAP-Cre line) results in GNP hyperplasia, whereas conditional deletion of Sufu after granule neuron specification (using the Atoh1-Cre line) does not lead to these defects (Jiwani et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiwani et al., 2020.

claim: Conditional deletion of Sufu in neural stem cells before granule neuron specification results in GNP hyperplasia.
source: Notably, the timing of SUFU LOF is critical; conditional deletion of Sufu in neural stem cells before granule neuron specification (using the hGFAP-Cre line) results in GNP hyperplasia, whereas conditional deletion of Sufu after granule neuron specification (using the Atoh1-Cre line) does not lead to these defects (Jiwani et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiwani et al., 2020.

claim: Conditional deletion of Sufu after granule neuron specification does not lead to GNP hyperplasia.
source: Notably, the timing of SUFU LOF is critical; conditional deletion of Sufu in neural stem cells before granule neuron specification (using the hGFAP-Cre line) results in GNP hyperplasia, whereas conditional deletion of Sufu after granule neuron specification (using the Atoh1-Cre line) does not lead to these defects (Jiwani et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiwani et al., 2020.

claim: SUFU-associated infantile MBSHH is a likely consequence of defects stemming from the early stages of granule neuron lineage specification at embryonic stages.
source: Thus, SUFU-associated infantile MBSHH is a likely consequence of defects stemming from the early stages of granule neuron lineage specification at embryonic stages.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing-dependent effects of Sufu deletion.

claim: Tumors initiated at embryonic stages are typically undetectable until several months after birth, when tumorigenesis has significantly progressed.
source: Unfortunately, tumors initiated at embryonic stages are typically undetectable until several months after birth, when tumorigenesis has significantly progressed.
evidence: This is general knowledge about tumor detection in pediatric cancers.

claim: Therapeutics for infantile MB must successfully curtail tumorigenic mechanisms at postnatal stages and minimally affect normal GNPs elsewhere in the cerebellum.
source: Thus, therapeutics for infantile MB must successfully curtail tumorigenic mechanisms at postnatal stages and minimally affect normal GNPs elsewhere in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a logical inference about therapeutic requirements.

claim: Inhibiting localized FGF5 and FGF signaling activity may provide new paths toward the design of targeted treatments.
source: Toward this goal, inhibiting localized FGF5 and FGF signaling activity may provide new paths toward the design of targeted treatments.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the rescue experiments.

claim: Measuring FGF5 may be a useful diagnostic biomarker for infantile MBSHH patients.
source: Since we confirmed the occurrence of high FGF5 levels in a subset of infantile MBSHH patients, measuring FGF5 may be a useful diagnostic biomarker for this patient population.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the FGF5 expression patterns in patient tumors.

claim: Detection of elevated FGF5 levels may identify patients who will be responsive to FGF-targeting treatments.
source: This may predict the lack of efficacy of SHH-targeting compounds in curtailing tumor growth but could instead significantly impede cerebellar development. Importantly, detection of elevated FGF5 levels may identify patients who will be responsive to FGF-targeting treatments.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the FGF5 expression patterns and rescue experiments.
